props.title: Valentine's Day
props.initialSlug: Love intertwines multiple LA couples on February 14th

sections.content: Valentine's Day (2010) follows the interconnected romantic ensemble format popularized by Love Actually (2003), but transplants the action to Los Angeles. Director Garry Marshall assembled an A-list cast including Julia Roberts, Bradley Cooper, and Anne Hathaway to weave together multiple love stories over a single February 14th. The film sparked a series of Marshall-directed holiday ensemble pieces, followed by New Year's Eve (2011) and Mother's Day (2016). While critically panned, these films tapped into audiences' appetite for star-studded romantic celebrations.

sections.content: The romantic ensemble comedy became a defining format of the 2000s, with films like He's Just Not That Into You (2009) and New Year's Eve (2011) following large casts through interweaving plotlines. These movies provided platforms for established stars while launching newer talents. Valentine's Day particularly showcased then-rising stars like Jessica Alba, Jessica Biel, and Taylor Swift in her film debut. The format allows exploration of different relationship stages - new love, long-term commitment, friendship turning romantic - while maintaining a light, commercial tone.

The holiday romance genre extends beyond ensemble pieces. Sleepless in Seattle (1993) used Valentine's Day as a pivotal plot point, while 50 First Dates (2004) and The Notebook (2004) became modern Valentine's classics. These films typically emphasize grand romantic gestures and idealized love stories, though some like (500) Days of Summer (2009) subvert traditional romance tropes. sections.content: While Valentine's Day represents the big-budget, star-driven romantic comedy of the 2000s, the genre has since shifted toward more grounded stories. Films like Crazy Rich Asians (2018) and To All the Boys I've Loved Before (2018) maintain romantic comedy conventions while incorporating greater cultural specificity and contemporary relationships. The ensemble format has largely moved to streaming series, allowing for deeper character development.
